Optional. Nothing in [Module 3](module3.qmd) assumes this page — it is the fourth
template, for the one question shape the three main templates cannot answer: **when
both of your variables are categorical.**

The t-test, ANOVA and regression on the Module 3 page all involve at least one
*continuous* variable. But plenty of research questions relate two **categories**:
does income band relate to whether a child feels safe in their neighbourhood? Do
boys and girls differ in how curious they are about alcohol? For those, you reach
for a **chi-squared (χ²) test of independence**, which asks whether the two
category systems are related or independent.

It follows the same template shape as the others — clean, visualise, check the
assumption, test, effect size, visualise the result — so if you have read one of
the Module 3 templates this will feel familiar.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

data <- readRDS("data/data.RDS")
```

## The question

**Is household income related to whether a child feels their neighbourhood is
safe?** Two categorical variables:

- `ab_g_dyn__cohort_income__hhold__3lvl` — household income in three bands
- `fc_y_nsc__ns_003` — the youth's response to a neighbourhood-safety item, on a
  five-point agree/disagree scale

## Clean

Two wrinkles here that the continuous templates did not have. First, both
variables carry the special codes `777` (*decline to answer*) and `999` (*don't
know*) — these are **not** points on the scale, so we drop them rather than let
them masquerade as responses. Second, a five-point scale crossed with three income
bands makes fifteen cells, and some will be nearly empty; we **collapse** the
safety item to three categories so every cell has enough data for the test to be
valid.

```{r}
#| label: chi-clean
clean <- data |>
  select(
    participant_id,
    session_id,
    family_id = ab_g_stc__design_id__fam,
    income    = ab_g_dyn__cohort_income__hhold__3lvl,
    safety    = fc_y_nsc__ns_003
  ) |>
  filter(session_id == "ses-00A") |>           # baseline only
  filter(!income %in% c(777, 999),             # drop "decline" / "don't know"
         !safety %in% c(777, 999)) |>
  mutate(
    income = factor(income,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c("< 50k", "50k to 100k", "> 100k")),
    # collapse the 5-point item into 3 so no cell is too sparse
    safety = case_when(
      safety %in% c(1, 2) ~ "Disagree",
      safety == 3         ~ "Neutral",
      safety %in% c(4, 5) ~ "Agree",
      .default = NA
    ),
    safety = factor(safety, levels = c("Disagree", "Neutral", "Agree"))
  )

clean <- clean[complete.cases(clean), ]
```

As on the main page, we keep one child per family so siblings are not counted as
independent observations:

```{r}
#| label: chi-independence
set.seed(1996)
clean_no_sibs <- clean |>
  group_by(family_id) |>
  slice_sample(n = 1) |>
  ungroup()
```

## The contingency table

A chi-squared test runs on a **cross-tabulation** — a grid of counts, one cell per
combination of the two variables. This table *is* the data for the test.

```{r}
#| label: chi-table
tab <- table(clean_no_sibs$income, clean_no_sibs$safety)
tab
```

Adding row proportions makes the pattern easier to see — what share of each income
band agrees their neighbourhood is safe:

```{r}
#| label: chi-proptable
round(prop.table(tab, margin = 1), 2)  # margin = 1 -> proportions within each income row
```

## Check the assumption

Chi-squared's main requirement is that **expected** counts are not too small — the
usual rule is that every expected count should be at least 5. The test stores the
expected counts, so we fit it once and inspect them.

```{r}
#| label: chi-expected
chi_check <- chisq.test(tab)
chi_check$expected  # all of these should be >= 5
```

If any expected count fell below 5, you would collapse categories further (as we
already did with the safety item) or use Fisher's exact test
(`fisher.test(tab)`) instead. Here they are comfortably above the threshold, so
the standard test is valid.

## Run the test

```{r}
#| label: chi-test
chi_result <- chisq.test(tab)
chi_result
```

Read it as: `X-squared` is the test statistic, `df` the degrees of freedom
`(rows − 1) × (columns − 1)`, and `p-value` whether to reject the null hypothesis
that income and perceived safety are **independent**. A p-value below 0.05 says
they are related.

## Effect size: Cramér's V

As always, significance is not size. **Cramér's V** rescales the chi-squared
statistic to run from 0 (no association) to 1 (perfect association), so it is
comparable across tables. A rough guide for a table with three levels on the
smaller side: 0.1 small, 0.3 medium, 0.5 large.

```{r}
#| label: chi-effect
n <- sum(tab)
k <- min(nrow(tab), ncol(tab))  # the smaller dimension
cramers_v <- sqrt(as.numeric(chi_result$statistic) / (n * (k - 1)))
cat("Cramér's V:", round(cramers_v, 3), "\n")
```

## Visualise the result

A grouped bar chart of the row proportions shows the association directly: the
taller the "Agree" bar climbs as income rises, the stronger the relationship.

```{r}
#| label: fig-chi-result
#| fig-cap: "Perceived neighbourhood safety by household income"
#| fig-alt: "Grouped bar chart of the proportion of children who disagree, are neutral, or agree that their neighbourhood is safe, within each of three income bands; the 'agree' proportion rises with income."
#| warning: false
plot_df <- clean_no_sibs |>
  count(income, safety) |>
  group_by(income) |>
  mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = income, y = prop, fill = safety)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", alpha = 0.85) +
  labs(
    title = "Perceived neighbourhood safety by household income",
    x = "Household income", y = "Proportion within income band", fill = "Feels safe?"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

## In short

The chi-squared test of independence is the categorical counterpart to the tests
on the main page:

- Build a **contingency table** of the two categorical variables.
- Check the **expected counts** are all at least 5 — collapse categories or use
  `fisher.test()` if not.
- Run `chisq.test()` and read the p-value.
- Report **Cramér's V** as the effect size, and show the pattern with a grouped
  bar chart.

Back to [Module 3](module3.qmd), or the downloadable
[`R_Template_chi.square.R`](../scripts/module3/R_Template_chi.square.R) to run this
on your own variables.
